objective: By the end of this lesson you can set best glide within ±10 knots, pick a field and fly a planned path to it, run the engine-failure checklist, and explain wind, density altitude, ELTs and the help ATC can give.
why: If the engine quits, the airplane becomes a glider. Pilots who fly best glide, pick a field early and stick to a plan walk away from forced landings.

prereading.what: Best glide, minimum sink, wind, gliding turns, common glide errors.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 3, 3-22 to 3-24

prereading.what: Power-off accuracy approaches and simulated emergency landings, the emergency checklist.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 9, 9-24 to 9-29

prereading.what: Types of emergency landings, psychological hazards, terrain selection, configuration, approach, engine failure after takeoff.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 18, 18-1 to 18-8

prereading.what: How density altitude, wind and speed change landing distance.
prereading.label: PHAK 11-17

prereading.what: Asking for help, radar help for VFR pilots, code 7700, ELTs, search and rescue.

warmup: Your engine quits at 3,000 ft AGL. You can see a long field behind you and a shorter one ahead into the wind. Which one, and how will you get there without power?

key_terms.def: Speed that gives the most distance for the altitude lost in still air. It occurs at L/DMAX.
Speed that loses altitude slowest, for the most time aloft. A few knots slower than best glide; less distance.
Highest lift-to-drag ratio. Least total drag.
An immediate landing, on or off an airport, because you can't keep flying (e.g., engine failure).
A point in the air from which you judge the rest of the power-off approach.
Constant-angle glide path to a set point, at constant airspeed and configuration.
Pressure altitude corrected for temperature. Higher DA means higher true airspeed at the same indicated airspeed.
Emergency locator transmitter. Sends a distress signal after a crash; 406 MHz units are detected by satellite.
Transponder emergency code. Sets off an alarm at radar facilities.

body.p: Memorize the immediate action items, then use the checklist [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]]. Fly first. Then try to fix it while you pick a field and plan [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

bullets: Above best glide? Hold altitude (or even climb) to slow, then lower the nose and trim for best glide [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
At or below best glide? Lower the nose at once to hold or regain best glide [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
Check flaps and gear are right for the situation [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
Pick a field and plan the approach [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

body.p: Critical items to check: fuel selector position, fuel quantity in that tank, fuel pressure (electric pump?), mixture, magneto switch, and carburetor heat [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

callout.text: Many real forced landings came from a fuel selector set to an empty tank. It may be wise to switch tanks even if the gauge shows fuel; gauges can be wrong [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

body.p: If the engine won't restart: switch the engine and fuel off just before touchdown. A cooled engine cuts the fire risk. Turn the master off, but only when you no longer need electrical power [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

check.q: Why change fuel tanks even if the gauge shows fuel in the selected tank?
check.a: Fuel gauges can be inaccurate, and many emergency landings came from a selector on an empty tank [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

body.p: Best glide speed gives the greatest forward distance for the altitude you lose, in still air. It occurs at the highest lift-to-drag ratio (L/D) [[24:83|AFH 3-22]]. Faster or slower adds drag and shortens the glide [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].

bullets: Weight doesn't change glide distance if you fly the right speed. A heavier airplane needs a higher speed and gets there sooner [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Drag items (flaps, gear, cowl flaps) steepen the glide. For max distance, clean up if you can [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Hold a constant glide speed. Speed changes ruin your judgment of glide distance and landing spot [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
Power off, pitch controls airspeed [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Trim once the speed is stable [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

callout.text: Never "stretch" a glide with back pressure below best glide. You'll land shorter, and you may stall [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

check.q: Two airplanes with the same L/D glide from the same altitude. One is heavier. Which glides farther?
check.a: Neither. Both cover the same distance; the heavier one flies faster and arrives sooner [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

chunks.title: Best glide vs minimum sink, and wind

head: Best glide
Minimum sink
rows: A few knots below best glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
You need to reach a field
Time matters more than distance, e.g. ditching at sea [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]

body.p: Wind: a tailwind makes you glide farther over the ground; a headwind, less far [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. In a headwind, a speed slightly above best glide can help you reach the aiming point [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].
Land into the wind if you can. Lower groundspeed means less energy to absorb: doubling groundspeed quadruples the destructive energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

Find the wind from a windsock, smoke, dust, brush fires, wind farms, or patterns on water [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. The crab you need on base also tells you the wind [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]. Place the base leg closer in a stronger headwind on final [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

check.q: You're trying to reach a field upwind. Will you glide farther or less far than in still air?
check.a: Less far, because the headwind lowers your groundspeed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

body.p: High density altitude: you land at the same indicated airspeed, but your true airspeed is higher. Higher groundspeed means a longer landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

Carburetor ice is most likely below 70°F with humidity above 80 percent, but can form up to 100°F and humidity as low as 50 percent [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]. It is especially dangerous at reduced power in a descent, and may not show up until you add power [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

callout.text: Simulated engine failure in carb-ice weather: carb heat full ON before closing the throttle, and open the throttle smoothly now and then to keep the engine warm [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]] [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

body.p: Over wide, smooth water or snow, you can lose depth perception (white-out in poor visibility). Risk: flying into the surface or stalling from too high [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

check.q: Why does a forced landing at a high-elevation field on a hot day take more distance?
check.a: Same indicated airspeed, but higher true airspeed and groundspeed, so the landing distance is longer [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

body.p: Your energy is altitude plus airspeed [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. With no thrust, drag drains that energy. You can descend at a constant airspeed, drawing on the energy stored as altitude [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].

A stabilized approach is a constant-angle glide path to a chosen point, at constant airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. Power off, the power is fixed at idle, and pitch controls airspeed [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Use any mix of straight glides and spirals to reach a normal key position at normal pattern altitude. From the key point on, fly a normal power-off approach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

bullets: Too high: slip, add flaps, move the base leg, or vary the turn to final [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. S-turns or a dog-leg also work [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].
Too low: never stretch the glide or retract flaps to reach the spot [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
Too fast is as bad as too slow: it causes floating and overshooting. You can't dive at a field and land on it [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
Save full flaps until you're sure you'll make the field [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
Aim past the numbers for a safety margin [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

callout.text: Energy mismanagement contributes to loss of control, CFIT and approach-and-landing accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

check.q: In a power-off glide, what controls your airspeed?
check.a: Pitch attitude; power is fixed at idle [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

chunks.title: Getting help: ATC, ELTs and search and rescue

body.p: Ask for help early. You're in at least an urgency condition the moment you doubt your position, fuel, weather, or anything else that affects safety [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

bullets: MAYDAY (distress) or PAN-PAN (urgency), each said three times. MAYDAY gets absolute priority and radio silence [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].
Use the frequency you're on, or 121.5 MHz. Most civil towers and radar facilities guard it [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].
Squawk 7700 if you can't reach ATC right away; it triggers an alarm at radar facilities [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]] [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]].
Radar facilities can give vectors to a VFR pilot in difficulty within radar coverage. It is advice; you are still responsible for flying safely [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].
Crash landing imminent: also give ELT status, landmarks, aircraft color, people on board and emergency equipment, and turn on the ELT if you can [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

head: ELT fact
Detail
rows: Stopped monitoring 121.5/243.0 on February 1, 2009. Only 406 MHz is detected by satellite [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]
Must be registered with NOAA. Has a 121.5 homing signal for searchers [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]
Replace (or recharge) after more than 1 cumulative hour of use, or at 50% of useful life [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]]
Analog: first 5 minutes after the hour, no more than three sweeps. No airborne tests [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]

body.p: Know how to turn the ELT on manually and check that it's transmitting [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]. Listen on 121.5 MHz before shutting down to catch a false alarm [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]. Renting? Consider a 406 MHz personal locator beacon [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

callout.text: File a flight plan and close it. If you don't report within one-half hour after your ETA, a search starts [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]. After a crash landing, stay with the airplane unless you have good reason not to [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]].

check.q: Why does a 406 MHz ELT bring help faster than a 121.5 MHz ELT?
check.a: Satellites detect 406 MHz almost instantly and the registration lets SAR verify quickly. 121.5 MHz signals are no longer monitored by satellite, so response may wait hours for confirmation [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

body.p: Generic AFH flow. Your POH speeds, flaps and checklist come first.

bullets: 1. Instructor closes the throttle and says "simulated emergency landing" [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Be clear who controls the throttle [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
2. Pitch for best glide (slow first if you're faster) and trim [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
3. Check flaps and gear for the situation [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
4. Pick a field within glide range. Weigh wind, field size and slope, and obstacles [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Point it out to the instructor [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
5. Plan the path: spiral or glide to a key position at pattern altitude, then a normal power-off approach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
6. Do the critical items and checklist, calling each one out [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

7. Prepare for landing as the evaluator asks: radio call, transponder, ELT, passengers, and the POH securing items (fuel, mixture, ignition, master) [[24:200|AFH 9-29]] [[24:353|AFH 18-4]] [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
8. Flaps once the field is assured; touch down at the lowest controllable airspeed [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].
9. Keep the engine warm and cleared [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. The approach ends when a safe landing is (or isn't) assured, never low enough to bother people or property on the ground [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.119(a): fly at an altitude that allows, if the engine fails, an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

check.q: What is the ACS airspeed tolerance for this task?
check.a: Recommended best glide airspeed ±10 knots (ACS PA.IX.B.S1).

head: Error
Fix
rows: Eagerness to get down: arriving too fast [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]
Hold best glide; lose extra height with turns or slips
Delaying the field choice at high altitude [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]
Pick a general area early, then refine
Stretching the glide with back pressure [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Hold best glide; pick a closer field
Set pitch by the horizon, then trim
Wait until the field is made
Fuel, mixture, mags, carb heat, every time
Skidding or slipping in gliding turns [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Not clearing for traffic in the descent [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Look in the turn direction and below

check.q: What does the AFH call one of the most common faults of inexperienced pilots in simulated emergency landings?
check.a: Eagerness to get down, arriving at the field too fast to land safely [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

chunks.title: Risk: choosing the field and sticking to the plan

body.p: Your choices depend on your route, your height, and extra airspeed you can trade for distance [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Up high, pick the general area first; ground looks different from altitude [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

bullets: Plan around wind, field size and slope, and obstacles on final. They rarely all agree [[24:353|AFH 18-4]] [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].
Hitting an obstacle at the end of the slide is far less dangerous than hitting one at flying speed. An unobstructed approach may beat an into-wind one [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].
Roads: watch for power and phone lines along them; look for the poles [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].
Don't pick a gap between trees that needs a steep descent [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].
Beyond gliding range of open ground? Choose terrain that absorbs energy, like crops or brush [[24:353|AFH 18-4]] [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

callout.text: Changing the plan: switch if a better field is clearly in reach, but generally change your mind only once [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Last-minute changes bring heavy maneuvering at low altitude [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

check.q: You chose a field at 3,000 ft AGL. At 1,500 ft you see a slightly longer one off to the side. Switch?
check.a: Only if it is obviously better and within reach; generally change your mind no more than once [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Avoid last-minute low-altitude maneuvering [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

chunks.title: Risk: stall, spin, CFIT, traffic and distraction

body.p: Low-altitude stall/spin: in a low gliding steep turn, too much rudder plus back pressure can turn into an unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. A cross-controlled stall almost certainly gives a rapid, unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

The desire to save the airplane leads to turning back with too little altitude or stretching the glide [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]. In the AFH's turn-back example, an engine fails at 300 ft AGL; after a 4-second reaction and 225° of standard-rate turning, the airplane ends up 1,016 ft below the runway [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

After a failure right after takeoff, straight ahead or a slight turn is usually the lowest-risk option [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. Students and low-time pilots should not attempt a low-altitude turn back [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
Configuration: flaps lower stall speed but add drag. Used too early, they can ruin a sound plan [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Follow the POH on gear position [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

Traffic: clear for traffic in the turn direction and the descent [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Distraction: doing the checklist and flying the approach at once is hard [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. Positive control on final comes before configuration and checklist tasks [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

check.q: On short final with the checklist unfinished, what has priority?
check.a: Positive airplane control. It has priority over configuration and checklist tasks [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

scenario.title: Silence over farm country
scenario.setup: You're cruising at 3,000 ft AGL on a humid 60°F morning in a carbureted trainer, on the left tank. The engine coughs, runs rough, then quits. Smoke from a farm chimney drifts east, so the wind is from the west. Ahead (west) is a short hay field. Behind you is a long plowed field next to a road. A student in another airplane is practicing somewhere nearby.

questions.a: Pitch for best glide (slow to it first if you're faster) and trim. Then run the critical items: fuel selector (switch tanks), fuel pressure, mixture, magnetos, carb heat [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

questions.q: Why is carb ice a real suspect today?
questions.a: Carb ice is most likely below 70°F with humidity above 80 percent [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]. The first sign with a fixed-pitch prop is an rpm drop, then roughness [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

questions.q: The short hay field ahead, into the wind, or the long plowed field behind you by the road?
questions.a: Into the wind keeps groundspeed and energy low [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]. The road field may have power lines along it [[24:354|AFH 18-5]]. Weigh wind, size, slope and obstacles [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

questions.q: At 1,000 ft you're high on base for the hay field. How do you fix it?
questions.a: Slip, add flaps, or adjust the base and the turn to final. Don't dive at the field [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

questions.q: What radio and transponder calls fit a real version of this?
questions.a: MAYDAY three times on your frequency or 121.5 MHz; squawk 7700 if you can't reach ATC; give ELT status and landmarks if a crash landing is imminent [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]] [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

questions.q: On short final you remember the master switch is still on. What now?
questions.a: Positive control comes first. Turn electrical power off only when you no longer need it [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

skills.do: Set and hold the recommended best glide speed ±10 knots.
skills.practice: Practice glides at altitude until you know the pitch picture, sound and feel; trim it off [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

skills.do: Configure the airplane per the POH/AFM and the conditions.
skills.practice: Clean for distance; flaps only once the field is made [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

skills.do: Pick a suitable field for altitude, wind, terrain, obstacles and glide distance.
skills.practice: On every flight, keep asking 'where would I land right now?' and note the wind [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

skills.do: Plan and fly a path to the field.
skills.practice: Fly 90° and 180° power-off approaches to build glide judgment [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

skills.do: Prepare for landing as the evaluator specifies.
skills.practice: Brief the steps before the flight: radio, transponder, ELT, passengers, securing the engine and fuel [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]] [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].
Chair-fly the POH engine-failure checklist; call out each item aloud [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

options: The greatest distance for altitude lost in still air
quiz.why: Best glide gives the greatest forward distance for a given loss of altitude in still air [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].

quiz.q: Compared with best glide, minimum sink speed is:
options: A few knots faster, more distance
A few knots slower, more time aloft but less distance
quiz.why: Minimum sink is lower than best glide; it maximizes time, with less distance [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

quiz.q: With a tailwind, your glide distance over the ground:
quiz.why: A tailwind raises groundspeed, so you glide farther [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

quiz.q: Engine fails while you're faster than best glide. You should:
options: Hold altitude or climb to slow to best glide, then lower the nose and trim
quiz.why: Above best glide, let the airplane slow (even climb) to best glide, then lower the nose and trim [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

quiz.q: The ACS airspeed tolerance for this task is:
quiz.why: Recommended best glide airspeed ±10 knots (ACS PA.IX.B.S1).

quiz.q: Doubling your groundspeed at touchdown does what to the destructive energy?
quiz.why: Doubling groundspeed quadruples the total destructive energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

quiz.q: Since 2009, which ELT signal is detected by satellite?
quiz.why: Satellite monitoring of 121.5/243.0 MHz stopped on February 1, 2009; 406 MHz is detected by satellite [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

quiz.q: During an emergency approach, what has priority over checklist tasks on final?
quiz.why: Positive control during the final part of the approach has priority over configuration and checklist tasks [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

takeaways: Fly first: best glide, trim, then pick a field.
Best glide = most distance; minimum sink = most time.
Headwind shortens the glide; land into the wind to cut groundspeed.
Plan to a key position; fix high with slips, flaps or path, never stretch low.
Fuel, mixture, mags, carb heat: check them every time.
MAYDAY, 121.5, 7700 and the ELT are your lifelines; file and close a flight plan.
cfi_notes: Say "simulated emergency landing" when closing the throttle, and agree who has the throttle [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
Let the student fly the chosen field until you end it, so they see the result of their errors [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
Watch for the student diving at the field, flaps too early, and skipping the critical items.
Terminate as soon as you know whether a safe landing was assured; respect 91.119 and people on the ground [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
Figure 18-5 labels the side offset 4,480 ft, while the AFH text says 4,200 ft. Teach the altitude-loss point, not the offset number.
Brief the simulated version of S5 (radio, transponder, ELT) so nothing real gets transmitted.
gaps: Best glide speed, flap settings and the engine-failure checklist are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM.
Sources do not quantify how density altitude changes glide distance; only landing distance and touchdown speed are covered.
The AFH turn-back example (Figure 18-5) shows 4,480 ft offset but its text says 4,200 ft.

activities.title: Best glide or minimum sink?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Most distance for the altitude you lose
Flown at the highest lift-to-drag ratio (L/DMAX)
Loses altitude at the slowest rate
A few knots slower than the other one
Useful when ditching at sea, where time matters more than distance
The speed to fly when you must reach a distant field

activities.title: True or false: calling for help

cards.s: A distress call should start with MAYDAY, said three times.
cards.why: Yes. Start with MAYDAY, preferably repeated three times. It gets absolute priority on the frequency [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

cards.s: Satellites still listen for 121.5 MHz ELT signals.
cards.why: No. Satellite monitoring of 121.5 and 243.0 MHz stopped on February 1, 2009. Only 406 MHz is picked up by satellite [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

cards.s: If you are already talking to ATC on an assigned code, switch to 7700 right away.
cards.why: No. Keep your assigned code while in radio contact, unless told otherwise. Use 7700 if you can't reach ATC right away [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

cards.s: Once ATC gives you radar vectors, the controller is responsible for flying you safely.
cards.why: No. Radar help to a VFR pilot is advice. You are still responsible for flying the airplane safely [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

cards.s: Once activated, an ELT should transmit for at least 48 hours.
cards.why: Yes. ELTs are built to run for at least 48 hours over a wide range of temperatures [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

cards.s: If you don't report within one-half hour after your ETA on a VFR flight plan, a search will be started.
cards.why: Yes. That is why you must close your flight plan when you arrive [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

activities.title: Fly the simulated forced landing
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Instructor closes the throttle and says "simulated emergency landing"
Slow to best glide if you're fast, then lower the nose and trim
Pick a field within gliding distance and point it out
Glide or spiral down to the key position at pattern altitude
From the key position, fly a normal power-off approach
Add full flaps once you're sure you'll make the field
Touch down at the lowest controllable airspeed

activities.title: Pick the field wisely
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then the best advice for it.

pairs.r: Watch for power lines; look for the poles
Skip it: it needs a steep descent
Aim for crops or brush to absorb energy
An unobstructed approach may be better, whatever the wind
Switch if it's in reach, but change your mind only once
Pick the general area first, then the exact spot

final_quiz.q: You're climbing out at 60 knots. Your airplane's best glide speed is 70 knots. The engine quits. What should you do first?
options: Lower the nose right away to get back to best glide
Hold the climb attitude to save altitude
Raise the nose to slow down further
final_quiz.why: If the failure happens at or below best glide, lower the nose at once to hold or regain best glide speed [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Holding the nose up below best glide makes you land shorter and can lead to a stall [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

final_quiz.q: Two airplanes have the same glide ratio but one is much lighter. Why does the lighter one use a lower best glide speed?
options: A light airplane stalls at a higher speed
A light airplane glides much farther at any speed
A light airplane reaches the same glide ratio at a lower airspeed
Light airplanes need more power to glide
final_quiz.why: A heavier airplane must fly faster to get the same glide ratio, so a lighter one uses a lower speed. Flown at the right speed, both glide the same distance [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

final_quiz.q: The engine quits with gear down and some flaps out. You need every foot of distance to reach the nearest field. What does the AFH advise?
options: Clean up drag items if you can, following the POH
Add full flaps to slow down
Lower the nose to gain speed and stretch the glide
final_quiz.why: Flaps, gear and cowl flaps add drag and steepen the glide. To get the most distance, remove drag-producing items if possible [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

final_quiz.q: You're gliding toward your aiming point into a strong headwind. Which speed choice can help you reach it?
final_quiz.why: In a headwind, a speed slightly above best glide can help you reach the aiming point [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. A headwind already shortens the glide over the ground [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

final_quiz.q: At a steady 9G stop, a light airplane needs about 9.4 feet to stop from 50 mph. About how far would it need from 100 mph?
final_quiz.why: Doubling the speed takes about four times the distance: about 37.6 feet [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]. That's why you touch down into the wind at the lowest controllable airspeed.

final_quiz.q: Your forced landing field is at about 5,000 feet elevation. Compared with a sea-level field, the minimum landing distance is about:
final_quiz.why: Minimum landing distance at 5,000 feet is 16 percent greater than at sea level. You land at the same indicated airspeed but a higher true airspeed [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

final_quiz.q: It's 55°F with high humidity, and your instructor is about to give you a simulated engine failure in a carbureted airplane. What should you do about carb heat?
options: Carb heat ON only after you pick a field
Partial carb heat once the engine gets rough
Full carb heat ON before the throttle is closed, and leave it on
No carb heat; it lowers power too much
final_quiz.why: When carb ice is likely and you expect closed-throttle flight, put carb heat full ON before closing the throttle and leave it on. Open the throttle smoothly now and then to keep the engine warm [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

final_quiz.q: At the key position you realize you're well too high for your field. Which is a proper fix?
options: Lower the nose and dive toward the field
Retract the flaps to reduce drag
Pick a farther field at low altitude
final_quiz.why: Slips, flaps, moving the base leg, and changing the turn to final correct for being high [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. You can't dive at a field and expect to land on it [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. Retracting flaps does the opposite: less drag flattens the glide and carries you even farther [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

final_quiz.q: You're choosing between two fields. One sits right next to a paved road. What hazard should you look for?
options: Soft dirt on the road shoulder
Power or telephone lines along the road
Road signs that block the windsock
Cars that will slow your rollout
final_quiz.why: Most highways and even dirt roads have power or telephone lines along them. Look for the poles to spot them in time [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].

final_quiz.q: Landing into the wind means flying over tall trees on final. The opposite direction is wide open. What does the AFH say?
options: Always land into the wind, no matter what
Clear the trees by slowing below best glide
An unobstructed approach may be better, even if not into the wind
final_quiz.why: It is sometimes better to plan the approach over an open area, whatever the wind. Hitting an obstacle at the end of the slide is much less dangerous than hitting one at flying speed [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].

final_quiz.q: As a student pilot, your engine fails at 400 feet AGL right after takeoff. What is usually the lowest-risk choice?
options: A standard-rate turn back to the runway
Pull up to gain altitude, then decide
A steep turn back to the runway
Land straight ahead or with a slight turn
final_quiz.why: Straight ahead or a slight turn is usually the safest option [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. A low-altitude turn back is an unacceptable risk for student and low-time pilots [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

final_quiz.q: The engine won't restart and you have the field made. When should you shut off the fuel and engine, and the master switch?
options: All of them as soon as the engine quits
Never; leave everything on for the landing
Fuel and engine just before touchdown; master only once you no longer need electrical power
Master first, then fuel once on the ground
final_quiz.why: Switch the engine and fuel off just before touchdown; a cooled engine lowers fire risk. Turn the master off only when you no longer need electrical power [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

final_quiz.q: You rent an airplane that has only a 121.5 MHz ELT. What does the AIM suggest?
options: Test the ELT in flight before each trip
Carry a 406 MHz personal locator beacon
Nothing; satellites will hear the 121.5 signal
Switch the ELT off to save the battery
final_quiz.why: Pilots who don't own the airplane should check its ELT and, as appropriate, get a 406 MHz personal locator beacon [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]. Satellites no longer monitor 121.5 MHz, and airborne ELT tests are not allowed [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].
